newsitem.title: USA: Sharp decline in US Treasuries pushes dlr lower. [CORRECTED 22:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Sharp decline in US Treasuries pushes dlr lower. [CORRECTED 22:30 GMT]

text.p: The dollar ended lower against the mark and the yen on Thursday, hurt by a sharp decline in the U.S. bond market, dealer said.

Treasuries were hit by a combination of pre-payrolls jitters, profit-taking and technical factors. Traders said much of the selling came from foreign investors and helped push the dollar lower against other major currencies.
"The dollar traded almost in lockstep with the bonds and the bonds got killed," said Alfonso Alejo, senior proprietary trader at Sakura Bank Ltd.
The greenback ended the session at 1.5495/00 marks, down from 1.5555/65 at the open. Against the yen, the dollar retreated as well, falling to 112.28/38 yen from 112.80/90 in early trade.

Contributing to the dollar's weakness against the yen was a rumor circulating overnight that influential Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara would call for a range of 108 to 110 in dollar/yen in a scheduled television interview.

Although Sakakibara, known as "Mr. Yen" for the impact his comments have had on the currency in the past, failed to confirm the rumor when he spoke on Japanese television later in the day, the dollar was unable to recover against the yen.
The dollar's downward drift against the deutschemark followed German data overnight which showed an increase in unemployment to a record high 10.7 percent in November.
Despite the weak data, and other recent signs of economic sluggishness in Germany, the Bundesbank did not cut interest rates at its council meeting on Thursday.
Although steady policy had been widely expected by the market, the central bank's decision did give the mark modest support, traders said.
Elsewhere, the pound stumbled overnight before recovering some of its losses in the U.S. session.
The overseas fall came after Bank of England Governor Eddie George downplayed the urgency for a British rate rise.
Expectations of a rate increase had helped push sterling to four-year peaks of 2.6370 marks and $1.6905 in recent weeks.
